_comment: These are APPLICATION permissions, not delegated ones. An app holding one
of these acts with no signed-in user: no MFA prompt, no Conditional Access
evaluation, and a sign-in log entry that does not look like a person. That
is why they are rated far above the equivalent delegated scope, and why
AAD-12.4 (which reads oauth2PermissionGrants, the DELEGATED consent table)
cannot see any of this — a malicious app-only grant returns zero rows from
Tier1 is tenant takeover: the permission can be used to obtain Global
Administrator, forge tokens for any user, or read every mailbox outright.
Tier2 is mass data access across all users without a takeover path.
A permission absent from both lists is reported in the inventory but is
not scored. Absence from this file is not a judgement that the permission
is safe — it means this catalogue has not rated it.

tier1.Why: Can assign directory roles, including Global Administrator, to any principal it chooses.
Can grant itself, or any other app, any application permission in the tenant. Self-escalation to everything below.
Can add credentials to any existing app registration, including ones that already hold privileged permissions, and then authenticate as them.
Broad write across the directory: users, groups, and their memberships.
Can add or federate a domain, which allows minting SAML tokens for any user in the tenant — bypassing MFA and every Conditional Access policy.
Can disable or weaken the Conditional Access policies the rest of this assessment measures.
Can replace any user's authentication methods, including registering an attacker-controlled MFA method.
Can alter Privileged Identity Management assignments and eligibility.
Can make a principal eligible for a privileged role.
Can schedule a privileged role assignment.
Exchange Online: full control of EVERY mailbox in the tenant. The single most direct path to mass mail exfiltration.
Exchange Online: app-only Exchange administration, including transport rules and mailbox delegation.
SharePoint: full control of every site collection, including permission changes.

tier2.Why: Read and modify mail in every mailbox.
Send mail as any user — the mechanism behind app-based business email compromise.
Create inbox rules in any mailbox, the usual persistence and exfiltration mechanism after a compromise.
Read and modify every file in OneDrive and SharePoint.
Read every file in OneDrive and SharePoint.
Read and modify content in every SharePoint site.
Read content in every SharePoint site.
Read and modify every user profile.
Read every user profile in the directory.
Read and modify every group, including membership of groups used for access control.
Modify membership of any group, including groups that grant access.
Read the entire directory — a complete reconnaissance view of the organisation.
Read every Teams chat message in the tenant.
Read every Teams channel message in the tenant.
Read and modify every user's calendar.
Read and modify device records, which Conditional Access device filters rely on.
